summary: Specifies how to carry Enhanced Variable Rate Wideband Codec (EVRC-WB) speech in RTP, and updates media type registrations for EVRC-B. It also defines a file format for storing EVRC-WB speech, such as in email. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a packing guide for sending a certain kind of compressed voice over the internet, plus a way to save it as a file.

subtitle: How to carry wideband EVRC-WB speech in RTP and in files, and what changes for EVRC-B media types.

tldr.problem: The EVRC-WB speech codec, a wideband extension of EVRC-B, needed a standard way to be sent over RTP and stored in files, and EVRC-B needed a way to signal its encoder and decoder modes.
tldr.mechanism: EVRC-WB reuses the EVRC-B packet formats (interleaved/bundled, header-free and compact bundle), registers new audio media subtypes, defines a file format, and adds SDP mode parameters. EVRC-B gains the optional parameters recvmode and sendmode.
tldr.outcome: Systems can negotiate EVRC-WB in SDP offers and fall back to EVRC-B. The RFC updates RFC 4788.

today: RFC 5188 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2008. It updates RFC 4788, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Background
sections.content:
This RFC specifies how to put EVRC-WB (Enhanced Variable Rate Wideband Codec) speech into the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP). It covers the header-free, interleaved/bundled and compact bundle packet formats, plus support for discontinuous transmission (DTX). It also updates the media type registrations for the EVRC-B codec.

EVRC-WB is a wideband extension of EVRC-B, developed in 3GPP2, and offers better speech quality than EVRC and EVRC-B. It can run in three modes (0, 4 and 7). Modes 4 and 7 are interoperable with EVRC-B. Mode 4 uses full-rate, 1/2-rate and 1/8-rate frames, and mode 7 uses only 1/2-rate and 1/8-rate frames. A mode change changes the output bit rate but causes no decoding problems, and the decoder does not need to know the encoder's current mode.

The target is packetized voice, most importantly IP telephony: IP phones, VoIP handsets, media gateways and voice messaging servers.
sections.plainLanguage: EVRC-WB is a way of squeezing voices so they sound clearer over the internet. This document says how to pack that squeezed voice into internet packets.

sections.title: EVRC-WB Frames
sections.content:
The codec works on 20-ms frames. The default sampling rate is 16 kHz, and 8 kHz input and output are also supported. Each frame comes out in one of three sizes: 171 bits, 80 bits or 16 bits. There are also two zero-bit frame types, blank (null) frames and erasure frames.

Each frame type has a value used in the Table of Contents (ToC). A full-rate frame takes 22 bytes, with 5 bits padded at the end. An erasure frame SHOULD NOT be transmitted by a sender.
sections.plainLanguage: The voice is cut into tiny 20-millisecond pieces. Loud, busy sounds need big pieces and quiet moments need small ones, so each piece is labeled with its size.

sections.title: RTP Header and Payload Formats
sections.content:
The RTP header is used as RFC 3550 specifies. The decoder does not need to know the sampling rate used at the encoder, and its output can be 8 kHz or 16 kHz either way. A 16-kHz RTP clock rate MUST always be used, and the RTP timestamp increases by 320 for each 20 milliseconds. The marker bit is set to 1 when the first frame in a packet is the first speech frame of a talkspurt, and to 0 otherwise.

Three packet formats are supported. Their details (ToC, interleaving, DTX and bundling) are exactly those of EVRC-B in RFC 4788, except that the mode change request field in the ToC MUST be read according to the RATE_REDUC parameter of EVRC-WB. The media type audio/EVRCWB maps to the interleaved/bundled format, audio/EVRCWB0 to the header-free format and audio/EVRCWB1 to the compact bundled format.

For congestion control, RFC 3550 and any applicable RTP profile apply. Packing more frames into each packet cuts the header overhead and the packet count, at the cost of more delay and less robustness to errors.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet is a small box that can hold several voice pieces. Fewer, fuller boxes waste less cardboard but make the listener wait longer for the first words.

sections.title: The Storage Format
sections.content:
For storing EVRC-WB speech, for example as a file or email attachment, the file starts with a magic number that identifies the vocoder. For EVRC-WB it is the ASCII string #!EVCWB\n.

The codec data frames follow in order, each prefixed by a single ToC entry extended to one octet by setting its four most significant bits to zero. A full-rate frame, ToC value 4, is stored as 0x04. Frames lost in transmission and frames not received MUST be stored as erasure frames (ToC value 5) so the file stays in sync with the original media.
sections.plainLanguage: A saved voice file starts with a secret label that says what kind of voice it is, then lists the pieces in order. If a piece went missing, a blank placeholder keeps everything lined up.

sections.title: Media Type Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers three new audio subtypes, EVRCWB, EVRCWB0 and EVRCWB1, and updates the audio/EVRCB and audio/EVRCB0 registrations from RFC 4788.

The EVRC-WB types share parameters such as mode-set-recv (a subset of modes 0, 4 and 7 the decoder prefers; absent means the set {0,4,7}) and sendmode (the encoder's current mode; absent means mode 0), along with the DTX parameters silencesupp, dtxmax, dtxmin and hangover. EVRCWB adds maxinterleave, which defaults to 5 when not signaled. EVRCWB1 adds fixedrate, with values 0.5 or 1, where 0.5 is assumed if absent.

EVRCWB0 and EVRCWB1 depend on RTP framing and are only for RTP transfer. They SHALL NOT be used for files, where audio/EVRCWB is used instead. The EVRCWB file extensions are evw and EVW.
sections.plainLanguage: Each way of packing the voice gets its own official name tag, so computers can tell them apart. Each tag also lists the settings you can choose.

sections.title: Mode Parameters and SDP Negotiation
sections.content:
sendmode lets a sender announce its encoder's current mode, and it can change mode at any time without trouble for the receiver. recvmode (EVRC-B) and mode-set-recv (EVRC-WB) let a decoder say which mode or modes it would like the sender to use. A sender MAY ignore them, and the receiver still decodes properly. The set {4,7} signals a preference for the narrowband modes of EVRC-WB.

The media subtype goes in the SDP a=rtpmap line, ptime and maxptime go in their own attributes, and other parameters go in a=fmtp as semicolon-separated pairs. In an offer, since EVRC-WB extends EVRC-B, the offerer SHOULD also list EVRC-B, with EVRC-WB preferred. An answerer that supports EVRC-WB keeps it, and one that supports only EVRC-B leaves just the EVRC-B payload type.

Other rules: mode-set-recv and sendmode are one-directional, and neither SHOULD be used where it is not useful (a sendonly or recvonly stream). With EVRCWB1, the whole session MUST use the same fixed rate and mode. Unknown parameters in an offer MUST be ignored and MUST NOT appear in the answer. For declarative SDP in SAP and RTSP, a participant MUST use the configuration provided.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a call, each side says what it can do. If the clearer voice works for both, they use it. If not, they fall back to the older voice type both understand.

sections.title: Compatibility with Legacy EVRC-B
sections.content:
This RFC adds the optional parameters recvmode and sendmode to the EVRC-B types audio/EVRCB and audio/EVRCB0, which is how it updates RFC 4788. Existing RFC 4788 implementations do not send these parameters and ignore them when received, so old and updated EVRC-B implementations interoperate.

The RFC walks through an offer from an updated implementation answered by a legacy one, and the reverse. In one example the answerer picks sendmode=4 although the offerer would accept mode 0, because recvmode is only a preference and the sender may send in a different mode.
sections.plainLanguage: New phones can add extra notes to their messages. Old phones just skip the notes they do not understand, so everyone can still talk.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Compression is applied end-to-end to the payload formats, and the encodings do not show significant non-uniformity. Implementations are therefore subject to all the security considerations of RFC 3558, plus those of RFC 3550 and any appropriate RTP profile such as RFC 3551. This RFC adds no new security mechanism of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is added here for safety. The same safety rules as for other voice-over-internet packets apply.

items.label: Full rate
items.desc: 22 bytes (171 bits, 5 bits padded at the end).

items.label: Erasure
items.desc: 0 bytes; SHOULD NOT be transmitted by a sender.
